english: which side are you on?; which do you go for?
use: Comes after two options to ask which camp someone is in; answer with ... ha kana.

example.romaji: raamen to udon nara, dotchi ha?
example.ja: ラーメンとうどんなら、どっち派？
example.english: Ramen or udon: which are you?

examplePolite.romaji: raamen to udon nara, dochira ha desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ラーメンとうどんなら、どちら派ですか？
examplePolite.english: Ramen or udon: which do you prefer?

polite: inu ha desu ka, neko ha desu ka?
politeJa: 犬派ですか、猫派ですか？
english: dog person or cat person?
use: A classic icebreaker; the same frame works for any pair: koohii ha? koucha ha?

example.romaji: nee, inu ha? neko ha? watashi wa zettai neko.
example.ja: ねえ、犬派？猫派？私は絶対猫。
example.english: Hey, dog person or cat person? I'm totally cats.

examplePolite.romaji: tokoro de, inu ha desu ka, neko ha desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ところで、犬派ですか、猫派ですか？
examplePolite.english: By the way, are you a dog person or a cat person?

notes: Answer inu ha, neko ha, or ryouhou suki (I like both).

english: I'm more of a homebody; I like staying in
use: Describes how you spend free time; the opposite is autodoa ha (outdoorsy).

example.romaji: watashi, kanzen ni indoa ha da yo. yasumi wa ie.
example.ja: 私、完全にインドア派だよ。休みは家。
example.english: I'm a total homebody. Days off, I'm at home.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa indoa ha desu. yasumi wa daitai ie ni imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 私はインドア派です。休みはだいたい家にいます。
examplePolite.english: I'm a homebody. On days off I'm usually at home.

notes: Light and friendly; hikikomori (shut-in) is a much stronger, negative word.

english: you look well; you seem good
use: Said on meeting someone after a while; reply un, genki da yo, or okagesama de in polite talk.

example.romaji: hisashiburi! sugoku genkisou da ne.
example.ja: 久しぶり！すごく元気そうだね。
example.english: Long time no see! You look great.

examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気そうですね。
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. You look well.

notes: -sou means 'looks like': tanoshisou (looks fun), oishisou (looks tasty).

src: 最近ちょっと太っちゃった
ja: 最近ちょっと太っちゃった
kana: さいきんちょっとふとっちゃった
politeJa: 最近ちょっと太ってしまいました
english: I've put on a bit of weight lately
use: Self-deprecating small talk about yourself; don't ask futotta? of others, it's rude.

example.romaji: shougatsu tabesugite, saikin chotto futotchatta.
example.ja: 正月食べすぎて、最近ちょっと太っちゃった。
example.english: I ate too much over New Year, so I've put on a bit of weight.

examplePolite.romaji: shougatsu ni tabesugite, chotto futotte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 正月に食べすぎて、ちょっと太ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I ate too much over New Year and put on a bit of weight.

notes: -chatta (from -te shimatta) adds an 'oops, it happened' feel.

english: have you lost weight?
use: A common compliment between friends after time apart; reply e, hontou? or sukoshi ne (a little).

example.romaji: are, yaseta? nanka sukkiri shita ne.
example.ja: あれ、痩せた？なんかすっきりしたね。
example.english: Oh, have you lost weight? You look trimmer.

examplePolite.romaji: are, yasemashita ka? sukkiri shimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、痩せましたか？すっきりしましたね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, have you lost weight? You look trimmer.

notes: Yaseta is the change; yaseteru (slim) describes a body type.

english: how many years has it been?
use: Said with surprise when meeting someone after years; answer with a guess like gonenburi kana.

example.romaji: uwa, hisashiburi! nannenburi? gonen kurai?
example.ja: うわ、久しぶり！何年ぶり？五年くらい？
example.english: Wow, long time! How long has it been? Five years?

examplePolite.romaji: sotsugyou irai desu ne. nannenburi deshou.
examplePolite.ja: 卒業以来ですね。何年ぶりでしょう。
examplePolite.english: Not since graduation, right? How many years has it been?

notes: -buri marks the time since last: mikkaburi (first time in three days), hisashiburi (in ages).

src: 前に言ってた〜、どうなった？
ja: 前に言ってた〜、どうなった？
kana: まえにいってた〜、どうなった？
polite: mae ni itte ita ..., dou narimashita ka?
politeJa: 前に言っていた〜、どうなりましたか？
english: how did that ... you mentioned turn out?
use: Follows up on something a friend told you last time: an interview, a date, a trip.

example.romaji: mae ni itteta mensetsu, dou natta? ukatta?
example.ja: 前に言ってた面接、どうなった？受かった？
example.english: How did that interview you mentioned go? Did you get it?

examplePolite.romaji: mae ni itte ita mensetsu, dou narimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 前に言っていた面接、どうなりましたか？
examplePolite.english: How did that interview you mentioned go?

notes: Itteta is short for itte ita (was saying); ano ken (that thing) can fill the gap.

politeJa: やっと落ち着きました
english: things have finally settled down
use: Said after a busy stretch such as a move, a project or a new baby, to say you're free again.

example.romaji: hikkoshi mo owatte, yatto ochitsuita yo.
example.ja: 引っ越しも終わって、やっと落ち着いたよ。
example.english: The move's done, so things have finally settled down.

examplePolite.ja: 引っ越しも終わって、やっと落ち着きました。
examplePolite.english: The move's done, so things have finally settled down.

notes: Ochitsuku also means 'to calm down': ochitsuite! (calm down!).

english: I moved house; I've moved
use: Shares news when catching up; say where with ni: yokohama ni hikkoshita n da.

example.romaji: jitsu wa, sengetsu yokohama ni hikkoshita n da.
example.ja: 実は、先月横浜に引っ越したんだ。
example.english: Actually, I moved to Yokohama last month.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa, sengetsu yokohama ni hikkoshita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 実は、先月横浜に引っ越したんです。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I moved to Yokohama last month.

notes: Hikkosu is the verb; hikkoshi is the move itself.

english: I ... for the first time in ages
use: Tells someone about doing something you hadn't done for a long time; any past verb fits the gap.

example.romaji: kinou, hisashiburi ni eigakan de eiga mita.
example.ja: 昨日、久しぶりに映画館で映画見た。
example.english: Yesterday I saw a film at the cinema for the first time in ages.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, hisashiburi ni eigakan ni ikimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、久しぶりに映画館に行きました。
examplePolite.english: Yesterday I went to the cinema for the first time in ages.

notes: Hisashiburi alone is 'long time no see'; with ni it goes before the verb.

english: I changed jobs
use: Shares job news when catching up; expect the follow-up doko ni? (where to?).

example.romaji: sou sou, haru ni tenshoku shita n da yo.
example.ja: そうそう、春に転職したんだよ。
example.english: Oh yeah, I changed jobs in the spring.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa, haru ni tenshoku shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 実は、春に転職したんです。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I changed jobs in the spring.

notes: Tenshoku means moving to a new employer; a transfer inside your company is idou or tenkin.

english: if it were me, I'd ...; if I were you, ...
use: Gives advice by saying what you'd do, which is softer than telling someone what to do.

example.romaji: watashi dattara, sugu yamechau kana.
example.ja: 私だったら、すぐ辞めちゃうかな。
example.english: If it were me, I'd quit right away.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi dattara, mou ichido hanashite mimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私だったら、もう一度話してみますね。
examplePolite.english: If it were me, I'd try talking to them once more.

notes: Men often say ore dattara or boku dattara; the line usually ends in kana or to omou.

politeJa: よくわからないですけど
english: I'm not really sure, but ...; I don't know much, but ...
use: Hedges an opinion or guess on a topic you don't know well.

example.romaji: yoku wakannai kedo, sore tabun daijoubu da yo.
example.ja: よくわかんないけど、それたぶん大丈夫だよ。
example.english: I'm not totally sure, but that's probably fine.

examplePolite.romaji: yoku wakaranai desu kedo, tabun daijoubu da to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: よくわからないですけど、たぶん大丈夫だと思います。
examplePolite.english: I'm not really sure, but I think it's probably fine.

notes: Wakannai is the spoken form of wakaranai.

english: personally; for me
use: Opens your own view and marks it as just your opinion; safe in any register.

example.romaji: kojinteki ni wa, mae no hou ga suki datta.
example.ja: 個人的には、前の方が好きだった。
example.english: Personally, I liked the old one better.

examplePolite.romaji: kojinteki ni wa, kono an ni sansei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 個人的には、この案に賛成です。
examplePolite.english: Personally, I'm in favour of this plan.

english: honestly; to be blunt; let's be real
use: Opens a frank admission among friends, often something people don't usually say out loud.

example.romaji: butchake, ano eiga tsumaranakatta yo ne.
example.ja: ぶっちゃけ、あの映画つまらなかったよね。
example.english: Honestly, that film was boring, wasn't it?

notes: Avoid with bosses or customers; shoujiki (honestly) is the neutral word.

english: for me; as far as I'm concerned
use: A casual, youthful way to give your own view.

example.romaji: watashi teki ni wa, kore de zenzen ii yo.
example.ja: 私的には、これで全然いいよ。
example.english: As far as I'm concerned, this is totally fine.

notes: Don't confuse it with shiteki (private), written the same; in polite talk use kojinteki ni wa.

english: honestly, genuinely; normally, as usual
use: In young people's speech it upgrades praise: futsuu ni oishii means 'actually tasty', not 'average'.

example.romaji: kore, futsuu ni oishii ne. bikkuri.
example.ja: これ、普通においしいね。びっくり。
example.english: This is actually really good. I'm surprised.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, futsuu ni oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、普通においしいですね。

notes: The older sense 'normally, in the usual way' is still common: futsuu ni aruite (just walk normally).

english: fairly; relatively; quite
use: Softens a description, often to say something is better than expected.

example.romaji: kono hen, warito shizuka de sumiyasui yo.
example.ja: この辺、わりと静かで住みやすいよ。
example.english: This area's fairly quiet and easy to live in.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hen wa warito shizuka desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この辺はわりと静かですよ。

notes: Wari ni means the same; kekkou is a bit stronger.

english: surprisingly; more than you'd think
use: Marks something that breaks your expectations, good or bad.

example.romaji: kono mise, igai to yasukatta ne.
example.ja: この店、意外と安かったね。
example.english: This place was surprisingly cheap.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, igai to yasukatta desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、意外と安かったですね。

notes: Igai ni means the same; igai na (unexpected) goes before a noun.
